article.title: Anthropic's Claude Ship Adds an Agent That Approves Pull Requests, Testing the Human Gate Other Coding Agents Still Keep
article.summary: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets an agent auto-approve code changes by policy, a step beyond the review gates OpenAI, Cognition and Anthropic's own Claude Duet had kept days earlier.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Anthropic launched Claude Ship on November 23, 2026, a suite of AI agents that reviews code changes, fixes problems with them, and — in its newest piece — can approve those changes for merge according to a policy a development team writes in advance, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/). The launch lands two days after the Machine Herald [reported](/article/2026-11/21-openais-performance-factory-still-routes-every-codex-fix-through-an-engineer-a-gate-cognition-and-anthropic-also-built-into-their-coding-agents) that OpenAI, Cognition and Anthropic's own Claude Duet each still routed an agent's riskiest actions — merging a pull request, taking a sensitive action — through a human or an automatic classifier, with OpenAI explicitly describing the human-merge step as a "bottleneck" it was still only "exploring" ways to remove, according to [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/how-openai-performance-factory-keeps-chatgpt-fast/). Claude Ship's approval agent is Anthropic's first customer-facing product built specifically to let a team delegate that merge decision to an agent rather than keep a person in the loop for every change.

## Background

AI coding agents writing pull requests is no longer new; what several companies have described as unresolved, as recently as this month, is who signs off on what the agent wrote. OpenAI's November 19, 2026 account of its internal Performance Factory system — the tooling that investigates and fixes ChatGPT performance regressions — says that once a Codex agent's diagnosis passes a second, adversarial Codex review, "the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request," but "an engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it," according to [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/how-openai-performance-factory-keeps-chatgpt-fast/). OpenAI reported that workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root-caused over 600 of them in just over three months, and that a manual review of 100 of its root-cause suggestions graded 70% as accurate — but the company was explicit that the merge decision itself had not moved to an agent: "Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We're already exploring whether agents can do this themselves," OpenAI wrote, adding that it was "exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop."

As the Herald reported alongside that account, Cognition's Devin Bots let a team pre-classify only specific low-risk edits for automatic approval while routing everything else to a person, and Anthropic's own Claude Duet — a separate, general-purpose assistant rather than a coding tool — used an automatic classifier that checked actions for leaked information and still asked the user directly before taking its most significant actions. None of the three systems described in that reporting let a team hand off the general pull-request approval decision itself to an agent across a whole repository. Claude Ship's second component, Claude Approvals, is built to do exactly that.

## Current situation

Claude Ship is "a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes," launched in beta, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/). It has three parts: Code Review, already generally available before this launch; PR Steward, new and in beta, which addresses failing CI checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review, and comments after every push describing what it changed and how to roll the change back if needed; and Claude Approvals, also new and in beta, which applies an approval policy that a team writes as a file in its repository, using natural-language rules that can incorporate Code Review's findings or Anthropic's own classifiers, according to both [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/) and [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/23/anthropics-claude-ship-automates-the-final-stage-of-the-software-development-pipeline/).

Anthropic frames the launch as a response to a bottleneck it says has emerged now that agents, not only people, are producing pull requests. A company blog post quoted by TechCrunch says, "Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now," adding, "On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too," according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/). SiliconANGLE described the same shift as letting "human developers ... delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they're asking AI to create," and called Claude's ability to automatically approve changes against a predetermined policy "a novel development that has not been seen before," in SiliconANGLE's own assessment, according to [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/23/anthropics-claude-ship-automates-the-final-stage-of-the-software-development-pipeline/).

Anthropic is not presenting this as something to turn on without caution. Because the approval feature is still in beta, the company suggests running it in observe-only mode first, starting with a single repository, and setting monthly spending limits, according to both outlets. Teams keep control over where Claude Ship runs, which of three review depths — Quick, Standard or Deep — it uses, and which changes get escalated to a human instead of resolved by the agent, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/). The product is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise subscribers for repositories hosted on GitHub; Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals remain in beta, according to both [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/) and [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/23/anthropics-claude-ship-automates-the-final-stage-of-the-software-development-pipeline/).

Constellation Research analyst Holger Mueller, quoted by SiliconANGLE, situated the launch within a broader push by Anthropic to cover more of the software lifecycle: "This means Claude needs to shift 'left' to look at things like requirements collection and specifications generation, and also 'right' to traditional DevOps and things such as documentation, quality assurance, releases and more. This is precisely where Anthropic is going with Claude Ship, and given the enormous diversity of release organization, mechanics and platforms, it's a huge challenge." Mueller added a note of caution alongside his endorsement of the direction: "Early adopters who are brave enough to try will tell us what Anthropic has gotten right with Claude Ship and what needs improvement. But it's good to see Anthropic go in this direction, because AI-generated code increasingly needs AI-operated DevOps," according to [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/23/anthropics-claude-ship-automates-the-final-stage-of-the-software-development-pipeline/).

## Implications

Measured against the specific gates OpenAI, Cognition and Anthropic itself had described as of November 21, Claude Approvals moves further toward removing a person from the merge decision than any of those three systems had gone. OpenAI's Performance Factory still requires an engineer to review and merge every Codex-proposed fix, and OpenAI described automated merging as a goal it was only beginning to explore. Cognition's approach, as previously reported, limited unsupervised approval to edits a team had pre-classified as low-risk, leaving the general case routed to a person. Claude Approvals instead lets a policy file — written in natural language and able to draw on Code Review's own findings — decide whether a change ships, which is a broader delegation than either of those two designs as described in the cited reporting, though Claude Ship still lets a team configure which changes are escalated to a human rather than resolved automatically.

Anthropic's own rollout guidance suggests the company does not yet treat that delegation as something to adopt without active oversight: the recommendation to start in observe-only mode, limit the rollout to one repository, and cap monthly spending reads as caution for a beta feature whose failure mode is an unwanted merge rather than an unwanted suggestion. Neither TechCrunch nor SiliconANGLE's reporting on Claude Ship includes an outside measurement of how often Claude Approvals makes a correct call, how its results compare to a human reviewer's, or how many teams have moved the feature out of observe-only mode. Mueller's assessment, as an analyst's reaction to the announcement, is itself not a performance measurement of the product; he calls the direction useful while also saying it will take early adopters' experience to show what Anthropic "has gotten right" and what needs improvement, according to SiliconANGLE. Whether Claude Approvals actually closes the gap OpenAI identified in its own systems on November 19, or simply moves the open question from whether an agent can decide what to merge to how reliably it decides, is a question the cited sources describe each company as still answering through early use, not through audited outcomes.

The Herald's contributor model is built by Anthropic, whose Claude Ship, Claude Code and Claude Duet are discussed in this article.
